summary:
H.R. 7198, the “Prove It Act of 2024,” amends chapter 6 of title 5, United States Code (the Regulatory Flexibility Act), to impose new procedural obligations on agencies and to create a petition mechanism by which small entities may challenge agency certifications that a proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

Section 2 amends 5 U.S.C. § 603(b) by adding a new paragraph (6) requiring that an initial regulatory flexibility analysis include, where feasible, any reasonably foreseeable indirect costs the proposed rule may impose on small entities, including entities that transact with directly regulated entities, are directly regulated by other governmental entities as a result of the rule, or are subject to other agency rules as a result of the rule. It amends § 605(b) to require an agency to publish its certification not later than 10 days after completing it. Section 2 also inserts new § 605A, which permits any small entity, group of small entities, or organization representing small entities to petition the SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy to review a § 605(b) certification. The Chief Counsel must determine the method, timing, and form of petitions and display that information on the Office of Advocacy website. A petition must contain specified identifying information, the problems with the certification, supporting data, a proposed solution, and an explanation. A petitioner may request a consultation, though the Chief Counsel may only explain process and assist in clarifying the petition, not advise on amendment or withdrawal. Upon receipt, the Chief Counsel makes a prima facie determination within 10 days: if the issues lack merit, the matter is closed; if they merit further review, the Chief Counsel informs the petitioner and the agency and proceeds to a full review. The full review requires the Chief Counsel to consider whether the agency correctly identified affected small entities, considered adequate economic data, and the economic implications of the rule, and to convene a meeting with the petitioner, agency representatives, and the OIRA Administrator. Within 30 days of commencing full review, the Chief Counsel must publish results in the Federal Register and on the Office of Advocacy website. If the Chief Counsel determines the proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the agency must perform initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses under §§ 603 and 604. If an agency fails to attend the required meeting or otherwise fails to assist, the final rule shall not apply to small entities. For judicial review under chapter 7, a challenged § 605(b) certification is deemed final agency action on the date the Chief Counsel determines no further review is warranted or publishes the full review results.

Section 3 amends 5 U.S.C. § 609 by adding subsection (f), which requires that for any rule an agency determines is likely to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the agency head shall publish on regulations.gov all guidance documents and interpretations of the rule and allow public comment.

Section 4 amends 5 U.S.C. § 610(b) to add a new factor (6) requiring consideration of indirect costs described in § 603(b)(6) and any other indirect costs arising during the 10-year review period. It also adds § 610(d), providing that if an agency fails to conduct a required periodic review within the 10-year period, the Chief Counsel shall notify the agency that the rule has ceased to be effective; the agency shall publish a Federal Register notice of cessation and solicit comments on reinstatement; and if the agency determines reinstatement is warranted, it shall have 180 days to complete the review, after which the rule is reinstated without regard to § 553 notice-and-comment procedures. This sunset mechanism applies to any final rule issued during the five years preceding enactment or on or after the date of enactment.
